results.result: K-fibers in HeLa metaphase cells contain approximately nine KMTs per kinetochore (8.5 ± 2.2, mean ±STD, n=292), as determined by large-scale electron tomography of three complete spindle reconstructions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C21 are directly supported by quantitative electron tomography data from three independent spindle reconstructions (Figure 3B, Table 3). The measurements are consistent across datasets with appropriate sample size (n=292 kinetochores) and statistical reporting (mean ±STD). This represents a major structural finding about k-fiber composition in human cells.

results.result: Only approximately half (49% ±15.5%) of KMT minus ends in HeLa metaphase spindles are positioned within the MT-centrosome interaction area (defined as 1.7 µm from the mother centriole), indicating that only half of KMTs directly reach the spindle pole while the other half are indirectly connected.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C31, C32, and C33 are supported by systematic analysis of KMT minus-end positioning relative to defined spindle pole boundaries (Figure 5C, Table 3). The MT-centrosome interaction area was objectively defined using Gaussian fitting to non-KMT minus-end distribution (C98). The finding that average KMT number at poles (4.1 ± 2.0) is approximately half that at kinetochores (8.5 ± 2.2) provides independent corroboration.

results.result: K-fibers exhibit substantial variation in circumference and KMT density along their length, with pole-proximal regions showing approximately 3-4 fold greater cross-sectional area compared to kinetochores and reduced KMT density (~64% of KMTs enclosed at poles vs. 100% at kinetochores).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C42, C43, C44, and C45 are supported by quantitative measurements of k-fiber cross-sectional polygonal areas and KMT density along the pole-to-kinetochore axis (Figure 7B, 7D, Table 4). The methodology for calculating polygonal areas using alpha-shape algorithm is clearly described. The broadening at poles is consistently observed across all three reconstructed spindles.

results.result: KMT associations with non-KMTs predominantly occur in spindle pole regions, with 60.7 ± 9.4% of KMT minus-end associations with MT lattices and 59.8 ± 6.7% of KMT lattice associations with other MT minus ends localized at poles (for 35 nm interaction distance).
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C46, C47, C48, and C50 are supported by systematic analysis of MT-MT associations at defined interaction distances (Figure 8A-C, Tables 6-9). The choice of 35 nm as an example interaction distance is justified by reference to dynein motor dimensions. The spatial distribution analysis is normalized by local MT density, addressing potential confounding by regional MT concentration differences.

results.result: KMTs display a broad length distribution with an average of 3.87 ± 1.98 µm (mean ±STD, n=2579), including both short KMTs (~20% <2 µm) and long KMTs (~39% longer than half-spindle length), confirming that KMTs within k-fibers have heterogeneous lengths.
results.evaluation: Claims C28, C29, C30, and C61 are supported by comprehensive length measurements of all KMTs across three spindle reconstructions (Figure 4A, Table 3). The broad distribution contrasts with a simple model of uniform KMT lengths and is consistent with previous observations in other systems (citations provided). The semi-automatic stitching methodology with manual verification (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) provides confidence in length measurements across section boundaries.

results.result: K-fibers in HeLa cells mediate a semi-direct connection with spindle poles, where at least some KMTs directly reach the poles while others are indirectly connected through associations with non-KMTs, similar to the pattern observed in C. elegans embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C62 and C63 are supported by integration of multiple lines of evidence: variable KMT lengths (C28), positioning of only ~50% of KMT minus ends at poles (C31), and preferential KMT-non-KMT associations at poles (C5). This interpretation is consistent with previous work (McDonald et al., 1992; O'Toole et al., 2020) and represents a synthesis of the structural data into a coherent model.

results.result: KMT tortuosity averages 1.1 ± 0.1 globally, with 62 ± 8% of KMTs showing tortuosity <1.1 (straighter). Tortuosity correlates with KMT length (R=0.68, p=2.2e-16) and position, with straight KMTs predominantly in the spindle center and curved KMTs at peripheral positions. Local tortuosity increases from kinetochores toward poles (R=-0.13, p=2.2e-16).
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C41 are supported by systematic tortuosity analysis of all KMTs (n=2579) using clearly defined metrics (Figure 6E-I, Tables 4-5). Both global and local (500 nm segments) tortuosity were measured. Statistical correlations are reported with appropriate p-values. The weak correlation of local tortuosity with position (R=-0.13) is appropriately characterized as weak but statistically significant given the large sample size.

results.result: The number of KMT attachments per kinetochore in metaphase is not influenced by inter-kinetochore distance (Pearson's R=0.04 and 0.29) or by k-fiber position within the spindle (central, intermediate, or peripheral regions show similar KMT numbers).
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C23, C77, and C78 are supported by correlation analysis (Figure 3C-D) and positional analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3N, Table 5). The lack of correlation with inter-kinetochore distance (R=0.04, 0.29) and similar KMT numbers across spindle positions indicate that KMT number is not simply determined by mechanical tension or geometric constraints. However, the analysis does not exclude other regulatory mechanisms.

results.result: At 35 nm interaction distance, each KMT associates on average with 10.6 ± 3.2 other MTs with average association length of 145 ± 186 nm, while each non-KMT associates with 7.4 ± 3.1 other MTs with average association length of 103 ± 118 nm. KMTs show higher numbers and lengths of associations compared to non-KMTs at increasing distances.
results.evaluation: Claims C52, C53, and C54 are supported by comprehensive analysis of MT-MT associations at multiple defined distances (Tables 10-11, Figure 9—figure supplement 2). The methodology of measuring associations in 20 nm segments with minimum 20 nm length is clearly described. The differential association patterns between KMTs and non-KMTs suggest distinct organizational principles.

results.result: Each reconstructed HeLa metaphase spindle contained approximately 6300 MTs (6278 ± 1614, mean ±STD) with pole-to-pole distance of 9.0 ± 1.7 µm, including 90-110 k-fibers with 859 ± 218 KMTs total, representing only ~14% of all spindle MTs.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C18 are supported by complete 3D reconstructions of three metaphase spindles (Table 1, Figure 2). The consistency across three independent spindles provides confidence in the measurements. The finding that KMTs represent only ~14% of total MTs but ~25% of tubulin mass (C67) is reconciled by the observation that KMTs are on average twice as long as non-KMTs (C68).

results.result: The number of KMTs per k-fiber in HeLa cells (~9) differs from PtK1 cells (~20), which may be related to differences in kinetochore size (HeLa: ~0.107 ± 0.075 µm², PtK1: 0.157 ± 0.045 µm²).
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 and C76 are supported by comparison of current data with previous studies (McDonald et al., 1992; McEwen et al., 1997, 1998a; Cherry et al., 1989). The indirect measurement of kinetochore area in HeLa cells (C59) is acknowledged as an estimate based on k-fiber cross-sections. The correlation between kinetochore size and KMT number is plausible but remains correlative rather than mechanistically established.

results.result: Centrally located KMTs are shorter with minus ends closer to the mother centriole compared to peripheral KMTs, likely related to the roundedness of mitotic spindles, indicating that k-fiber position within the spindle affects individual KMT ultrastructure.
results.evaluation: Claims C64, C65, and C83 are supported by positional analysis of KMTs (Figure 5—figure supplement 4, Table 5). The interpretation that this relates to spindle roundedness (C65) is presented as inference with supporting citation (Taubenberger et al., 2020). This represents an interesting observation about spatial heterogeneity in KMT organization, though the mechanistic basis remains speculative.

results.result: Non-KMTs have an average length of 2.0 ± 1.7 µm (mean ±STD, n=14458) with high numbers of very short MTs, and 38 ± 9% of non-KMT minus ends are localized in the MT-centrosome interaction zone.
results.evaluation: Claims C34 and C35 are supported by comprehensive measurements of non-KMTs across three spindles (Figure 4B, Figure 5E, Table 3). The exponential length distribution of non-KMTs contrasts with the broader distribution of KMTs and is consistent with dynamic instability kinetics (C71). The lower percentage of non-KMT minus ends at poles compared to KMTs (38% vs 49%) supports distinct organizational principles.

results.result: The average kinetochore area (indirectly measured) is 0.10 ± 0.07 µm² with KMT density of 112 ± 60 KMTs/µm² and average center-to-center KMT spacing of 74 ± 22 nm (corresponding to ~50 nm wall-to-wall spacing).
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by measurements of k-fiber cross-sections at kinetochores (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-E, Tables 3-4). The indirect measurement approach (encircling KMTs) is clearly described and appropriate given the difficulty of directly visualizing kinetochores in cryo-fixed material. The wall-to-wall spacing calculation (C27) appropriately accounts for MT diameter.

results.result: The majority of annotated KMTs displayed open flared ends at the kinetochore, consistent with previous observations on KMT plus-end morphology in mammalian cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C19 is supported by visual inspection of tomographic data (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and is consistent with previous work (McIntosh et al., 2013). The flared morphology is characteristic of growing or stable MT plus ends at kinetochores. This represents a confirmatory observation rather than a novel finding.

results.result: The average distance between sister k-fiber ends (median KMT plus-end positions) is 1.13 ± 0.24 µm (mean ±STD, n=292).
results.evaluation: Claim C20 is supported by measurements from all three datasets (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D). This measurement serves as a validation that the three spindles were captured at similar metaphase stages, supporting the appropriateness of pooling data across spindles for comparative analysis.

results.result: On average 42 ± 8% of KMT lattices are associated with either KMT or non-KMT minus ends at 35 nm distance, while only 39.1 ± 4.6% of non-KMT lattices show such associations, with the majority being associations with non-KMT minus ends.
results.evaluation: Claims C49 and C51 are supported by reciprocal analysis of MT minus-end associations with KMT lattices (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C-F, Tables 8-9). This provides a complementary view to the minus-end-centric analysis and confirms that KMTs preferentially interact with other MTs compared to non-KMTs.

results.result: The KMT length distribution in HeLa cells is strikingly similar to distributions obtained by biophysical modeling with light microscopy and to distributions in C. elegans embryos. KMTs are on average twice as long as non-KMTs, and while KMTs represent ~14% of MT number, they account for ~25% of tubulin mass.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C70 are supported by comparison with parallel study (Conway et al., 2022) and previous work (Redemann et al., 2017). The reconciliation of MT number percentage (~14%) with tubulin mass percentage (~25%) through the observation that KMTs are twice as long as non-KMTs (C68) demonstrates internal consistency of the measurements.

results.result: The exponential length distribution of non-KMTs is typical of dynamic instability kinetics, while the broader KMT length distribution indicates different dynamics and possibly higher stability of plus-ends against depolymerization, suggesting KMTs have distinct properties from non-KMTs.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 are supported by comparison of length distributions (Figure 4) and citations to previous work on MT dynamics (Burbank et al., 2007; Loiodice et al., 2019). The interpretation is reasonable but remains inferential, as the study provides structural snapshots rather than dynamic measurements. The conclusion is consistent with known properties of kinetochore-attached MTs.

results.result: Cold-treated cells show cold-stable k-fibers while most non-KMTs depolymerize, and KMTs are likely stabilized by interaction with kinetochores and/or by KMT-KMT/KMT-non-KMT associations possibly mediated by MT-associated proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C74 and C75 are supported by citation to previous work (Maiato et al., 2004) and represent reasonable speculation about mechanisms underlying the observed structural differences between KMTs and non-KMTs. However, the current study does not directly test these mechanisms, so this remains interpretive.

results.result: Many KMTs are relatively short (~20% <2 µm) and only 5% of k-fibers have no KMTs in the MT-centrosome interaction area. In C. elegans, only ~20% of KMT minus ends were within 2 µm of the mother centriole, suggesting most KMTs do not contact centrosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 are supported by analysis of KMT length distributions and minus-end positioning (Figure 4A, Figure 5—figure supplement 3). The comparison with C. elegans (C81-C82) draws on previous work to support the generality of semi-direct k-fiber organization across species. The finding that 95% of k-fibers have at least one KMT reaching the pole (C80) is important for the semi-direct connection model.

results.result: Increased KMT tortuosity at spindle poles might promote anchoring of broadened k-fibers into the non-KMT network through MT-MT interactions. KMTs show high tendency to associate with non-KMTs at poles, while non-KMTs show flat association patterns at 25-35 nm but increased central associations at 35-50 nm distances.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C88 are supported by integration of tortuosity measurements (C41) with MT-MT association analysis (Figures 8-9). The interpretation that increased tortuosity promotes anchoring (C84) is speculative but reasonable. The differential spatial patterns of KMT vs non-KMT associations (C86-C88) are well-documented and suggest distinct organizational principles.

results.result: Integration with parallel light microscopy study suggests KMTs predominantly nucleate at kinetochores and grow toward poles along well-aligned trajectories, with spindles exhibiting properties of active liquid crystals (high nematic order S=0.81±0.02 near chromosomes, lower S=0.54±0.02 at poles). K-fiber broadening at poles may result from decreased structural organization of surrounding non-KMTs.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C95 are supported by reference to parallel study (Conway et al., 2022) that combines the current EM data with light microscopy and modeling. The liquid crystal framework (C91) is supported by citations to theoretical work (Brugués and Needleman, 2014; Oriola et al., 2020). The correlation between k-fiber broadening and decreased nematic order (C95) represents reasonable speculation integrating multiple observations.

results.result: The area of the outer kinetochore might indirectly define the size and/or number of available free binding sites for MTs.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is presented as speculation with supporting citations (Drpic et al., 2018; Monda and Cheeseman, 2018). While the correlation between kinetochore size and KMT number is observed (C55-C59), the current study does not establish a mechanistic link. This remains a plausible hypothesis requiring further investigation.

results.result: Mitotic spindles can contain thousands of MTs, but only a fraction is associated with kinetochores. These kinetochore microtubules (KMTs) function to establish physical connections between chromosomes and the rest of the spindle.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8 represent established background knowledge supported by citations to previous work (Redemann et al., 2017; Flemming, 1879; Khodjakov et al., 1997; Maiato et al., 2004; Musacchio and Desai, 2017; Rieder, 1981; Rieder and Salmon, 1998). These are contextual claims that frame the study rather than novel findings.

results.result: Previous studies reported k-fibers in PtK1 cells contain ~20 KMTs, RPE1 cells contain 12.6±1.7 KMTs per k-fiber, and different cell types exhibit variation in chromosome sizes that could modulate KMT numbers. KMT organization varies across species from single KMTs in budding yeast to multiple KMTs in organized k-fiber bundles in human cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C14 represent accurate summaries of previous literature (McDonald et al., 1992; McEwen et al., 1997; O'Toole et al., 2020; Moens, 1979; Winey et al., 1995; Oegema et al., 2001; O'Toole et al., 2003; Redemann et al., 2017; Begley et al., 2021; Godek et al., 2015). These provide important context for interpreting the current findings.

results.result: Methodological details: HeLa cells were cultured in DMEM with 10% FBS and antibiotics; samples were frozen at ~2000 bar with cooling rate ~20000°C/s; MT-centrosome interaction area was defined as 1.7 µm from mother centriole; MTs within 100 nm of tomogram borders were excluded (<1% of total).
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C100 describe methodological details that are clearly documented in the Materials and Methods section. The high-pressure freezing parameters (C97) are supported by citation (Reipert et al., 2004). The definition of MT-centrosome interaction area (C98) is based on objective Gaussian fitting. The exclusion criteria (C99-C100) are appropriate and have minimal impact (<1%).

results.result: The authors report that k-fibers in HeLa metaphase cells contain approximately 9 KMTs per kinetochore (8.5 ± 2.2, mean ±STD, n=292), based on electron tomography reconstructions of three complete spindles.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised this work as 'an incredible resource for cell biologists' and noted the 'sophisticated reconstructions.' While reviewers requested additional EM images to support conclusions and raised methodological concerns about section collapse and MT tracking errors, they did not challenge the core KMT number finding itself. The data was accepted after corrections were made.

results.result: The authors claim that only about half (49% ±15.5%) of KMT minus ends reach the spindle pole (defined as within 1.7 µm MT-centrosome interaction area), with the average number of KMTs per k-fiber at the pole (4.1 ± 2.0) being lower than at the kinetochore (8.5 ± 2.2), suggesting a semi-direct connection model.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised significant concerns about this interpretation. Reviewer 1 noted that 'the fact that so many KMTs do actually reach the pole is important and surprising to me' and questioned the arbitrary nature of the 1.7 µm cutoff definition. Reviewer 3 questioned whether the 40% of minus ends away from poles reflects 'poor MT tracking' and requested error analysis. Reviewers also noted that previous EM studies already showed semi-direct connections in mammalian spindles, questioning the novelty of this claim.

results.result: K-fibers show variation in circumference and KMT density along their length, with broadening at the pole-proximal side: the polygonal area is ~3-4 fold higher at poles compared to kinetochores, and only 64% of KMTs remain enclosed in the k-fiber circle at poles versus nearly 100% at kinetochores.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding but requested better motivation and clearer explanation. Reviewer 2 noted 'the polygon area analysis shown in Figure 6–supplement 1D is unclear and difficult to follow' and 'they did not address our comment that the polygon area analysis is never motivated or explained.' Despite requests for clarification, the core observation of k-fiber broadening was not disputed.

results.result: KMT associations with other MTs (both KMTs and non-KMTs) occur predominantly at spindle poles: 60.7 ± 9.4% of KMT minus-end associations with MT lattices and 59.8 ± 6.7% of KMT lattice associations with other MT minus ends were observed at poles (for 35 nm interaction distance).
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised major concerns about this conclusion. Reviewer 1 extensively critiqued that 'the preference for KMTs to have non-KMTs as neighbors near the pole...is uncorrected for two structural issues: the increased density of MTs near the poles...and the fact that there are many more non-KMT in this region.' Reviewer 1 insisted on normalization for MT density before making claims about preferential interactions. Reviewer 3 similarly noted 'the increased MT associations towards the pole can reflect simply this increased MT density.' The authors were required to normalize the data, which changed the interpretation.

results.result: KMTs display variable tortuosity (average 1.1 ± 0.1) that correlates with length (R=0.68) and position: straight KMTs (<1.1 tortuosity) are predominantly central while curved KMTs (>1.1) are peripheral, and local tortuosity increases from kinetochores toward poles (R=-0.13).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the tortuosity measurements but requested better motivation. Reviewer 2 stated 'A different motivation is needed for the tortuosity analysis. Tortuosity reports on microtubule curvature, but NOT twist–it doesn't tell us anything about 3D helicity.' Reviewer 1 suggested the title 'K-fibers are broadened at spindle poles' was 'a bit of an exaggeration' and preferred 'widening' over 'splaying.' Despite these concerns about framing, the quantitative tortuosity data itself was not challenged.

results.result: Each HeLa metaphase spindle contains approximately 6300 MTs (6278 ± 1614) with pole-to-pole distance of 9.0 ± 1.7 µm, including 90-110 k-fibers with 859 ± 218 KMTs total, representing only ~14% of all MTs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about the spindle length measurement. Reviewer 2 noted 'HeLa spindle lengths were previously reported to be ~12 µm, however, here they are reported to be significantly shorter in all spindles analyzed. The authors should clarify the origin of this discrepancy.' This suggests potential systematic measurement issues. Reviewer 1 also requested the discrepancy between 14% MT number versus 24% tubulin mass be explained, which was addressed by noting KMTs are longer on average.

results.result: The number of KMT attachments per kinetochore in metaphase is independent of both inter-kinetochore distance (Pearson's R=0.04-0.29) and k-fiber position within the spindle (central vs. intermediate vs. peripheral).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these negative correlation findings. Reviewer 2 requested clarification of 'the motivation for comparing inter-kinetochore distance and the number of MTs at the kinetochore, and what previous evidence might suggest a correlation,' but the statistical analysis itself was accepted.

results.result: KMTs have an average length of 3.87 ± 1.98 µm with broad distribution (20% <2 µm, 39% >half-spindle length), while non-KMTs are shorter (2.0 ± 1.7 µm average) with exponential distribution favoring very short MTs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these length measurements and noted they confirm previous observations. Reviewer 1 stated the data is 'in good agreement with Cherry's observations' and that length distributions are 'strikingly similar to the distribution obtained by biophysical modeling in combination with light microscopy.' Reviewer 3 requested analysis of whether MT ends could be generated by breaking, but did not challenge the length measurements themselves.

results.result: At 35 nm MT-MT distance, each KMT associates with 10.6 ± 3.2 other MTs with average association length of 145 ± 186 nm, while non-KMTs associate with 7.4 ± 3.1 other MTs with 103 ± 118 nm average length; KMTs show higher association numbers and lengths at increasing distances.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these quantitative measurements but requested clarification. Reviewer 1 noted 'you state that the number of associations was 10.6, but it is not clear what this number means. Number/KMT, per k-fiber or what?' The measurements themselves were not disputed, only their presentation needed improvement.

results.result: K-fibers in HeLa cells mediate a semi-direct connection with spindle poles where at least one KMT directly reaches the pole while others are indirectly linked to non-KMTs, similar to the anchoring pattern observed in C. elegans spindles.
results.evaluation: Reviewers challenged the novelty and framing of this conclusion. Reviewer 2 stated 'Previous EM studies in mammalian spindles have already shown that k-fibers form semi-direct connections to the pole' and suggested authors 'provide more context as to why their main point about a semi-direct connection between kinetochores and poles in human cells is novel and exciting.' Reviewer 1 noted the 'textbook models proposed and challenged in the text are not representative of the common understanding in the state of the field.'

results.result: The KMT length distribution in HeLa cells is strikingly similar to biophysical modeling predictions and to C. elegans embryos; KMTs are twice as long as non-KMTs on average, and the data supports a model where KMTs predominantly nucleate at kinetochores and grow toward poles.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these comparative analyses and integration with the parallel Conway et al. study. Reviewer 1 noted 'the addition of https://cfci.shinyapps.io/ASGA_3DViewer/ as a viewer tool is a major step in data sharing' and that the paper 'is now an excellent contribution to the literature.' However, Reviewer 1 cautioned that 'the statement that these and related data show that KMTs nucleate predominantly at kinetochores is true only for metaphase cells, and this limitation must be stated.'

results.result: KMTs display open flared ends at kinetochores; the average kinetochore area is 0.10 ± 0.07 µm² with KMT density of 112 ± 60 KMTs/µm² and center-to-center spacing of 74 ± 22 nm (corresponding to ~50 nm wall-to-wall spacing).
results.evaluation: Reviewers questioned the kinetochore size measurements. Reviewer 1 noted 'you estimated the size of each kinetochore by the area occupied by the KMTs...you then go on to calculate the correlation between the number of KMTs and the size of the area they occupy and get a great correlation. But this is not meaningful. Of course, you get a good correlation because you are estimating the size of the kinetochore by the area occupied by the MTs.' This circular reasoning undermines confidence in the kinetochore area measurements.

results.result: The difference in KMT number between HeLa cells (~9 KMTs) and PtK1 cells (~20 KMTs) correlates with kinetochore size differences (HeLa: 0.107 ± 0.075 µm² vs. PtK1: 0.157 ± 0.045 µm²), suggesting kinetochore area may define available MT binding sites.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this comparative analysis and interpretation. The discussion contextualizes the findings within previous literature on different cell types. No specific concerns were raised about this comparison, though the kinetochore size measurement method was questioned elsewhere.

results.result: Central KMTs are shorter with minus ends closer to the mother centriole compared to peripheral KMTs, likely related to the roundedness of mitotic spindles, suggesting k-fiber position affects individual KMT ultrastructure.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this positional analysis. Reviewer 2 requested the authors 'explain the significance of finding more KMT minus-ends at spindle poles in central k-fibers compared to peripheral k-fibers' and 'consider plotting KMT length versus kinetochore region,' which was addressed. The finding itself was not disputed.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on C1 and C21 regarding KMT number per kinetochore. Both evaluations find the quantitative electron tomography data supporting these claims. Reviewers praised the work as 'an incredible resource' and accepted the core finding despite requesting additional methodological details.

Significant disagreement on C2, C31, C32, C33 regarding KMT minus-end positioning at poles. OpenEval finds claims supported by systematic analysis, but peer reviewers raised major concerns about arbitrary cutoff definitions, potential MT tracking errors, and questioned novelty since previous EM studies showed semi-direct connections in mammalian spindles.

Agreement on C3, C4, C42-C45 regarding k-fiber broadening at poles. Both evaluations accept the core finding. Peer reviewers requested better motivation and clearer explanation of polygon area analysis, but did not dispute the quantitative observations.

Major disagreement on C5, C46-C48, C50 regarding preferential KMT-non-KMT associations at poles. OpenEval finds claims supported with density normalization, but peer reviewers extensively critiqued the lack of proper normalization for MT density and structural confounds. Authors were required to normalize data, which changed interpretation.

Agreement on C36-C41 regarding tortuosity measurements. Both evaluations accept the quantitative data. Peer reviewers requested better motivation and clarified that tortuosity measures curvature not twist, and suggested 'widening' over 'splaying' terminology, but did not challenge the measurements themselves.

Disagreement on C62-C63 regarding semi-direct k-fiber organization model. OpenEval finds the synthesis of multiple evidence lines supporting this interpretation, but peer reviewers challenged novelty, noting previous EM studies already showed semi-direct connections in mammalian spindles and questioned whether textbook models being challenged are representative of current understanding.

Partial disagreement on C15-C18 regarding spindle dimensions. OpenEval finds measurements consistent across datasets, but peer reviewers raised concerns about spindle length being significantly shorter than previously reported (~12 μm), requesting clarification of this discrepancy and suggesting potential systematic measurement issues.

Agreement on C52-C54 regarding MT-MT association measurements. Both evaluations accept the quantitative data. Peer reviewers requested clarification on what association numbers represent (per KMT, per k-fiber, etc.) but did not dispute the measurements themselves.

Agreement on C64-C65, C83 regarding positional variation in KMT organization. Both evaluations accept the findings. Peer reviewers requested explanation of significance and suggested additional analyses (KMT length versus kinetochore region), which were addressed, but the core observation was not disputed.

Agreement on C28-C30 regarding broad KMT length distribution. Both evaluations accept these measurements as confirming previous observations. Peer reviewers noted data is 'in good agreement with Cherry's observations' and 'strikingly similar' to biophysical modeling results.

Agreement on C22-C23 regarding lack of correlation between KMT number and inter-kinetochore distance. Both evaluations accept the statistical analysis. Peer reviewers requested clarification of motivation for the comparison but did not challenge the findings.

Significant disagreement on C24-C27 regarding kinetochore size measurements. OpenEval finds the indirect measurement approach appropriate, but peer reviewers identified circular reasoning: estimating kinetochore size by KMT area and then correlating KMT number with that area produces meaningless correlation. This undermines confidence in kinetochore area measurements.

Agreement on C55-C59, C76 regarding comparative analysis across species. Both evaluations accept this contextual analysis within previous literature. The correlation between kinetochore size and KMT number is accepted, though the measurement method for kinetochore size was questioned elsewhere.

Agreement on C66-C69 regarding reconciliation of MT number versus tubulin mass percentages and integration with Conway et al. parallel study. Both evaluations accept the comparative analysis. Peer reviewers praised data sharing tools and noted the paper is 'an excellent contribution,' but cautioned that KMT nucleation claims apply only to metaphase cells.

Partial overlap on C49, C51 regarding reciprocal MT minus-end association analysis. OpenEval finds this complementary analysis supporting preferential KMT interactions, but peer reviewers' concerns about density normalization (discussed for C5, C46-C48, C50) also apply to these related claims.

Partial overlap on C34 regarding non-KMT length distribution. OpenEval discusses comprehensive non-KMT measurements including exponential length distribution, while peer reviewers accepted length measurements and noted agreement with previous observations. Only C34 overlaps between these result sets.

Minimal overlap on C19 regarding flared MT plus-end morphology at kinetochores. OpenEval notes this as confirmatory observation consistent with previous work. Peer reviewers did not specifically comment on this finding, though R12 addresses other kinetochore-related measurements.

Minimal overlap on C60 regarding mechanistic speculation about kinetochore size determining KMT number. OpenEval rates this as UNCERTAIN speculation, while peer reviewers accepted the comparative analysis context but questioned the kinetochore size measurement method elsewhere.

Minimal overlap on C89 regarding integration with Conway et al. parallel study. OpenEval discusses liquid crystal framework and nematic order (C89-C95), while peer reviewers focused on data integration and sharing tools, with only C89 overlapping between these result sets.
